title: Binary to Gray Code Converter: how it works, formula and examples

The [Binary to Gray Code Converter](/binary-to-gray-code-converter) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Convert binary to Gray code and back — one bit changes at a time. Enter your binary number (0s and 1s) and direction and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Convert between binary and Gray code — the reflected binary code where each step changes only one bit. Binary 1010 (decimal 10) becomes Gray 1111; counting in Gray code goes 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100, with a single bit flipping at every step. That property is why Gray code is used in rotary encoders, analog-to-digital converters and error correction: a misread bit can only move the value by one step, never by a large jump.

## How to use the Binary to Gray Code Converter

Start by typing or pasting your binary number (0s and 1s), then choosing your direction from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter a binary number using only 0s and 1s.
2. Choose binary to Gray code, or Gray code to binary.
3. Read the converted value — leading zeros are kept so the width matches.

## Formula

Binary to Gray: gray = binary XOR (binary shifted right by 1). Gray to binary: repeatedly XOR the result with itself shifted right until the shift is zero.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Binary to Gray Code Converter](/binary-to-gray-code-converter) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. Binary 1010 is decimal 10. Shifted right by one it is 0101; XOR gives 1111, so the Gray code is 1111. Converting 1111 back gives 1010 again. ## Why one bit at a time matters

In ordinary binary, counting from 7 (0111) to 8 (1000) flips all four bits at once. If a sensor reads the bits during the change, it can briefly see any combination — 0111, 1111, 0000 — and report a wildly wrong position. In Gray code, 7 is 0100 and 8 is 1100: only the first bit changes, so a mid-change read can only ever be one step out. That is why position encoders and analog-to-digital converters use Gray code.

## Gray code counting

Gray code counting is a cycle: for three bits it runs 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100, then back to 000 with one bit changing — including the wrap from the last value back to the first. This reflected pattern is generated by mirroring the previous sequence and prefixing 1s, which is why it is also called reflected binary code.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- The Gray code of a number always has the same number of bits — leading zeros are kept.
- Binary and Gray share the first bit: the most significant bit never changes.
- Use Gray code wherever a sensor reads a changing value — a glitch can only shift it by one step.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is Gray code?

A binary numbering where consecutive values differ by exactly one bit. It is used in rotary encoders and converters so a misread can only move the value by one step. Try it with your own numbers in the [Binary to Gray Code Converter](/binary-to-gray-code-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How do you convert binary to Gray code?

XOR the binary number with itself shifted right by one bit. 1010 XOR 0101 = 1111, so binary 1010 becomes Gray code 1111. Try it with your own numbers in the [Binary to Gray Code Converter](/binary-to-gray-code-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the Gray code of 0?

0 — the Gray code of 0000 is 0000. The most significant bit is always the same in binary and Gray code. Try it with your own numbers in the [Binary to Gray Code Converter](/binary-to-gray-code-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Binary to Gray Code Converter use?

Binary to Gray: gray = binary XOR (binary shifted right by 1). Gray to binary: repeatedly XOR the result with itself shifted right until the shift is zero.
